NIST publishes battery-safety reference standards; participants in standards-setting work would appear in NIST workshop attendee lists.
creative_extensions.expected_observable: UL-certified products listing KULR as mfr; NIST workshop participation
creative_extensions.signal_direction: absence of UL listings while claiming commercial Li-ion safety products is moderate contradiction; presence is corroboration

creative_extensions.source_label: TAM source quality audit
creative_extensions.endpoint_or_method: Internal review — Precedence Research / Market and Markets Research / CoherentMI are paid TAM-vendor reports; cross-check claims against authoritative sources (DOE, BloombergNEF, BNEF Battery Outlook)
creative_extensions.rationale: Citing 'private space exploration market $1.1T by 2030' from CoherentMI is a TAM-inflation signal — CoherentMI is a low-rigor market-research aggregator. BNEF / IEA / DOE projections are typically 5-10x lower. TAM-source quality is itself diagnostic of management's marketing tendencies.
creative_extensions.expected_observable: comparison of CoherentMI projection vs IEA/DOE 2030 space-economy figures
creative_extensions.signal_direction: TAM cited from low-rigor source while ignoring authoritative source = marketing-inflation signal

claims.extraction_notes: Taxonomy cell consumer_products/safety_compliance is GAP — proposed connectors cpsc_recalls* and cpsc_certifications* not built. CPSC isn't the right regulator anyway for industrial Li-ion battery products (CPSC covers consumer goods; KULR's products target industrial/aerospace customers). m_source_status=NONE because there's no clean catalog test, BUT creative_extensions span 4 high-value sources (DOT/PHMSA, FAA hazmat, UL Product iQ, NIST/BNEF TAM benchmark) that the executor should log for backlog promotion. TAM-source-quality audit is non-traditional but is a real interpretable signal of management posture toward marketing inflation.
